title: Batteries and a power budget
summary: Bench-test the rover's two motors and H-bridge, measure current at no load, light load and a stall, then size the battery from the numbers.
materials: two geared DC motors with quadrature encoders

steps.title: Ask, imagine, plan
steps.body:
A new season opens with the rover you build from scratch: ask, imagine, plan, build, test, fix.

Ask: how long will a battery actually keep the rover driving? A battery label promises a number, but the motors' own current draw decides what that number turns into.

Imagine: two geared motors and a dual H-bridge driver, both wired to an ESP32, on the bench before any chassis exists. Measure how hard they pull on the battery, then the label's number turns into real minutes.

Plan: on paper, sketch three conditions to test: the motors spinning free, the wheels lightly loaded against the table, and one wheel briefly held still. Decide where the multimeter breaks into the circuit so it reads current, not voltage.

figure.alt: Three horizontal bars compare motor current at spinning free (about 70 milliamps), light load (about 150 milliamps), and a brief stall (over 500 milliamps, a 5 to 8 times spike) because stalling removes the motor's back-push against the current.

items.s: Stall removes the back-push; current spikes 5-8x

steps.title: A motor brakes its own current
steps.body:
While a motor spins, it also pushes back against the very current that drives it, like a pump fighting water that is already flowing.

That push grows with speed and limits how much current the battery has to supply. Stop the shaft from turning, at a stall, and the push disappears completely.

With the push gone, the battery drives current through almost nothing but the motor's bare wire resistance. Current jumps far past the no-load or light-load reading, often five to eight times higher.

A typical small gear motor like this one might draw about 70 milliamps spinning free and 150 milliamps under light load. A brief stall on the same motor can spike past 500 milliamps, which is why the stall test only lasts a second or two.

figure.alt: A formula diagram: battery capacity 2000 milliamp-hours divided by two motors' light-load draw of about 300 milliamps equals a predicted 6.7 hours of runtime. Below, one 20-minute rover session is compared against that 6.7 hour budget, more than twenty times longer than one session needs.

steps.title: The power budget: capacity divided by draw
steps.body:
A battery's capacity is measured in milliamp-hours, written mAh, for the rover's 2S pack.

Capacity divided by draw gives hours. Two motors together might draw about 300 milliamps under light load, twice the single-motor figure above. A 2000 milliamp-hour battery divided by that 300 milliamp draw predicts about 6.7 hours of driving: 2000 divided by 300 is 6.67.

This season's rover sessions run about 20 minutes at a time, a third of an hour. The predicted 6.7 hours is more than twenty times what one session needs, so the battery is not the limiting factor today.

A brief stall spends charge fast but does not last, so it barely dents the budget. The real cost is any long stall, which the bug diary below asks you to avoid.

figure.alt: A left-to-right wiring diagram: the 2S battery feeds a multimeter wired in series (breaking the loop to read milliamps), which feeds the dual H-bridge driver, which drives Motor L and Motor R; the ESP32 sends drive signals to the H-bridge on a separate control line.

items.s: Bench wiring: multimeter in series to read current

steps.title: Measure three conditions on the bench
steps.body:
Wire the two motors to the H-bridge driver, and the H-bridge to the ESP32 and the battery, with nothing else attached yet.

Break the circuit between the battery and the rest of the wiring. Wire the multimeter in series so current has to pass through it to get anywhere. Set the meter to read current in milliamps.

Measure three conditions, three runs each, nine readings in total. First, both motors spinning free with the wheels off and nothing touching the shafts. Second, wheels pressed onto the shafts and resting lightly on the table so friction lightly loads them. Third, one wheel held still by hand so its motor stalls.

Ask an adult to stand by for the stalled-wheel test. Free the wheel again within a couple of seconds each time, and never hold a stall longer than that.

Write the median of each condition's three readings on your graph paper sketch. Then use the light-load figure with the science step's formula to predict how many hours a fresh battery should last.
checklist: The multimeter was wired in series, breaking the loop, not across two points
An adult was present for every stalled-wheel reading and each stall lasted only a couple of seconds
All three conditions were measured three times each, nine readings in total
A predicted runtime in hours was calculated from the light-load current using capacity divided by draw

steps.title: Load condition versus current draw
steps.body:
The motors, the battery and the wiring stay the same for every row. Only the condition changes: spinning free, lightly loaded, or one wheel stalled.

Test each condition three times, nine rows in total. For each run, write the condition and the current the multimeter read in milliamps.
steps.question: Which condition drew the most current, and about how many milliamps more was that than spinning free?

steps.title: Bug diary
steps.body:
One line for each thing that did not work the first time and what you tried. Classics this week: the multimeter left set to read voltage, which never breaks into the loop and reads nothing useful.

Also watch for a stall held too long, which can warm the motor and drain the battery faster than the real test called for. And watch for a loose wire at the battery holder, which reads current as zero even though the rover's brain is clearly powered.

steps.title: Show it
steps.prompt: Photo of the multimeter wired in series during the light-load test, next to your graph paper sketch with all nine readings and the predicted runtime

extras.title: What is inside the battery running your rover
extras.body:
Find out how your battery's voltage actually sags under load, not just what the label promises.

Predict first: write in the Maker's Log what you expect the battery's voltage to do under load compared with sitting idle.

Measure it with the week's own kit. Set the multimeter to volts and read the battery's voltage with the rover off, then again while both motors drive under light load.

Compare: line up the idle reading and the loaded reading side by side, and write the gap in volts.

Teach it: explain to the family why a battery stores a chemical reaction, not electricity itself. Say why that reaction struggles to keep up once its ingredients run low.
